text.p: These are the leading stories in the Sarajevo press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) reduced security measures in the divided southern town of Mostar. They had been reinforced after Moslem-Croat clashes last week.

- Haris Silajdzic, co-chairman of Bosnia's collective cabinet, met U.S. official charged with economic issues in Bosnia Claude Genz. Silajdzic hopes Bosnia will remain in the focus of U.S. attention and stresses a significant role for the U.S. representative in economic reconstruction in Bosnia.

- Sweden is likely to provide 40,000 houses to Bosnia in exchange for Bosnian exports. The project also includes a joint enterprise with Swedish technology and 10,000 to 12,000 new jobs for Bosnian workers, the Swedish ambassador said.

- Ejup-Ganic, vice-president of the Moslem-Croat federation and federal minister for refugees and displaced persons, visited Bosnia's troubled town of Mostar and discussed the current situation with local officials.
- Sarajevo's Army House hosted a one-day exhibition of military equipment on Wednesday.
- Air Commerce, a state-run air company, will start regular commercial flights between Sarajevo and Berlin on February 22, Sarajevo's news agency ONASA said.

- Local authorities in Mostar start working on 1.5 billion mark project in Mostar "free zone" in the south part of the town. The project will include the construction of new infrastructure and a modern telecommunications system.
- Bosnia's collective presidency is due to meet on Friday or Monday, newspaper's sources say. The presidency will meet after two weeks' break.
- The bodies of nine soldiers who were killed during an offensive in 1993 were exhumed in the Sarajevo suburb of Hrasnica on Wednesday.
- Bosnia's shadow government formed of opposition parties is due to be inaugurated on March 3 in Sarajevo.

- Pope John Paul II's visit to Sarajevo set for April 13 will be a chance to show in a good light the region and people once proclaimed as a source of hatred and conflicts, a cleric board said on Tuesday.
- Sarajevo psychiatrists expect a considerable rise of suicide attempts in the city caused by war trauma.

- Sarajevo's catholic church of St. Anthony was stoned on Tuesday. Local police reported only material damage. More than a hundred worshippers were attending mass at the time of the incident, which police said was a result of the political situation and negative media influence.

- A foreign terrorist group has been broken after one member, Italian Carlo Mazzoni, was arrested by police in central Bosnian town of Zenica. Other terrorists are still in hiding, Zenica police said.
